utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis with Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, Aleksandar Aleksic for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is no reason to delay us, could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to begin this morning by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I just want to remind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, good morning to you. Before Mr. Hannis resumes his cross-examination, I want to remind you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to begin this morning by looking at your report. I see you have a copy of it in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to be a little picky in part because you are an expert, and I think the first exhibit I showed you, you -- which was a document from the commander of the reserve police station in Blazuj, you gratuitously pointed out some problems with his writing, his style, his improper use of abbreviation, so I think it's only fair that we look at some of those things in connection with your report. First of all, if you would look at the page setting out the contents, I guess it's page 2 of your report. And we see you have five, I don't know what would you call them, five chapters of your report? Or sections, I don't know how you would call those?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see they are numbered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- but the way you phrase your question, there's just something I need to clarify in my own mind from the witness. Mr. Bajagic, the report to which Mr. Hannis has just referred when -- I'm relying on my own recollection of the testimony at whatever day it was last week where you pointed out the style, the -- certain other references of the report in question, did I correctly understand your testimony to be that because of those things that you observed you had doubts about the authenticity of that report? Was that the point you were making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that wasn't my point. The point was that the official name of the institution as mentioned in the heading was wrong. As far as I remember, it read police station of public security, whereas it should be public security station. There is a -- a term was used that should not be there according to the rules and regulations. That's what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that for me. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Professor, what would you call those five items, are they chapters of your report or sections? I want to use the proper term.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can call them chapters. The chapters of the report or the sections of the report, there's not much of a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll look at this page and we'll see the chapters are numbered 1, 2, 2 again, 3, and 4. I take it that was just a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably a mistake. If you use Microsoft Word to draft a document, then you can make a mistake if you don't click on the right icon, but you can see how many chapters there are merely by looking at this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I note that within the body of the report chapter -- the second chapter 2 here that's described as "The functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of BH" is listed at page 51 in the English as chapter 3 as it appears to be, but the next chapter, "Rules on internal organisation," at page 130 of the English is also listed as chapter 3. Is that another Microsoft problem?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a problem of numbering. When you use Microsoft Word, that can happen. There are five chapters but the numbering can get out of hand and the result is as we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. You make several references to Professor Nielsen's report, and I note that you've misspelled his name a few times; for example, at paragraph 95 in footnotes 119, 121, and 130. And at first I thought perhaps that that is a function of the fact that Serbian is primarily what I would call a phonetic language, but in other places in your report you have his name spelled correctly. Was that a Microsoft problem or an error on your part?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a problem when you type, sometimes you are bound to make a technical error when typing. These things happen. I told you that the report contains some technical errors, maybe some letters are missing, maybe there are some superfluous matters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Letters, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these mistakes are no more serious than perhaps a letter, here or there, or a comma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Another thing I noted that I wanted to ask you about has to do with the use of a terminology and consistency in the use of terminology. In paragraphs 291 through 334 of your report, you are talking a lot about the role of the MUP in connection with prison camps, and sometimes you speak of prisoner of war camps and then sometimes that seems to just sort of drift into prison camps. Can you tell the Court your understanding or your definition of the difference between the following: A prisoner of war camp, a prison camp, a collection centre, and an investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many documents I cited in my footnotes also contain different terminology depending on the situation, probably. So the documents that I used are inconsistent, terminologically. When I say POW camp, it's logical to assume that in those camps there were people who were taken prisoner in combat. Some documents I use -- also use the term investigation centres or reception centres, and I merely -- I merely use the same terms. It wasn't my intention to confuse anybody with inconsistent terminology. I merely adhered to the sources. And often I put the terms in inverted commas because it was my wish to be as specific as possible when analysing a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you take a look at paragraph 299 in your report. I think that's page 95 of the B/C/S and page 112 of the English. That paragraph reads: "The previous paragraph shows that the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH was in charge of and responsible for all matters that concerned the setting up of prison camps and the organisation of life in these camps, from capturing people and bringing them to the camps and centres to the release, prosecution, et cetera." Now, it's been my understanding that the army was primarily responsible for prisoner of war camps and other types of camps or collection centres or detention facilities were places where non-prisoners of war were being held, that is civilians, women and children, non-combatants; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was responsible for the majority of these facilities, whatever we choose to call them. POW camps and also some other categories of facilities. From the analysis of the documents mentioned in -- or dealt with in the previous paragraph, I drew a summary conclusion which you can find in paragraph 299, and I analysed the documents in the previous paragraphs depending on the availability of documents. Of course there were also other situation, namely that the municipal authorities, that is Crisis Staffs in some situations had authority over such centres. But in most cases when we speak about prisoners of war, everything that had to do with them was in the responsible of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with you about prisoners of war, but in your answer at page 6, line 3, you said: "POW camps and also some other categories of facilities." You said: "The army was responsible for the majority of these facilities." Please, Professor, can you precisely tell me what other categories of facilities other than prisoner of war camps are you talking about? Can you give me the name describing them, tell me the type of individuals held there, and the particular provision of law that made the military responsible for such facilities other than prisoner of war camps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said that in some situations the Crisis Staffs as the municipal authorities had authority over some camps or centres or whatever they called them, collection centres where there were civilians who were not taken prisoners, that they had jurisdiction over these. I didn't specifically mention the army but I was speaking about the municipal authorities and that's also what I mentioned in these paragraphs of this chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I beg to differ with you. In your previous answer, you said: "The army was responsible for the majority of these facilities, whatever we choose to call them." But now let me ask you about Crisis Staffs. Can you tell me in what provision of the law or the constitution was it established that the Crisis Staffs had authority over these collection centres and other types of detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know with regard to Crisis Staffs the chronology of their establishment and how their names changed to War Presidencies or war commissions, and finally they were again called Executive Boards. But I didn't deal with the functioning of the Crisis Staffs in the RS, I analysed the MUP. I didn't deal with Crisis Staffs to the same level of detail as with the MUP. Of course, it's important to mention the Crisis Staffs and know how they changed until they got their old names again and that is the Executive Board, but I didn't analyse the legal foundations or, indeed, all matters that pertained to the Crisis Staffs. And that wasn't my task either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but you just said in your answer at page 6, line 23, that, "The Crisis Staffs as the municipal authorities had authority over some camps and centres." And my question was: Where or upon what do you base that? Where in the law or the constitution or anywhere else does it say that Crisis Staffs have authority over those facilities? Can you point me to a legal provision or is that just your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't speaking about legal provisions. The constitution doesn't mention that. I spoke about documents based on the analysis of which I drew the conclusion that in some municipalities the Crisis Staffs had authority or jurisdiction about such facilities. I didn't say I found that in laws and regulation, but I arrived at that conclusion by analysing documents that speak about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, if we turn the questions around which Mr. Hannis has just put to you, could I ask you then if the MUP, of which you are an expert, if the MUP were responsible and had jurisdiction for any centre or place where detainees were kept, be it civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MUP under the laws and regulations was not the institution that had jurisdiction over these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that is the de jure answer to my question. Was it also a de facto situation that in no instance did the MUP or the police stations, either the centres or the stations, have any responsibility or jurisdiction over any centre or place where detainees were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As one can see from the analysis in my expert report, I deal with the problem of the link between the MUP and such situations in some chapters of my report. The MUP was not fully responsible for anything that can be called a prison camp or especially the collection centres, but the situation on the ground was such that the territorial units of the MUP had problems with this category of persons precisely because of the orders that they received from the Crisis Staffs or some unresolved issues with the VRS in relation to their general activities regarding these categories of persons, be it the provision of security or anything else that the organs of the MUP were tasked with sometimes. In spite of that, the MUP didn't often raise this issue and apply for a resolution of the problem because they were reluctant to meddle with such things, and I state as much in some of my paragraphs, but it may be best to be more particular by analysing some paragraphs. In paragraph 297, I mention Crisis Staffs, and in some other paragraphs, too, I openly state that the MUP, in reality, had problems with these things and that such a situation existed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could the witness be reminded to speak a bit slower pace, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic -- yes, thank you. Please remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, the reason I put these questions to you is that your report is not completely clear or at least the reading of it does not provide the answers with a great deal of accuracy. What do you mean when you said to us just awhile ago that the MUP was not fully responsible for anything that can be called a prison camp or especially the collection centres? What do you mean when you say that the MUP was not fully responsible? Your answer suggests that the MUP was in part responsible for these centres. How is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not speaking literally in terms of responsible, but the MUP did not have authority over such camps anywhere as the Army of Republika Srpska did. There are documents, instructions showing that it is the military organs that are in charge of such facilities carrying out tasks in a certain territory. A public security station or its members or members of the crime prevention police received tasks that were related to such categories of persons. That's what I said, and that pertained to the uniform police and the crime police that was not in uniform, but it's not that they were like the military, the army, who were in charge of all aspects of life as far as these centres are concerned. So I spoke from that point of view. They carried out certain tasks and they carried out certain activities, but it's not that the Ministry of the Interior as an institution was in charge as the Army of Republika Srpska was, or rather, military organs in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what were those tasks that the police performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were situations when the members of the Ministry of the Interior were re-subordinated to military organs and when they took part in securing such facilities. There were situations when members of the Ministry of the Interior in accordance with their powers according to the law and what indeed is the jurisdiction of the ministry, they took part in collecting information. There were such situations where members of the Ministry of the Interior, together with military investigative organs, took part in collecting information, or rather, interrogating such persons in the sense of collecting information about war crimes or any other matters that may be of relevance to security. Those are the situations where most frequently members of the Ministry of the Interior carried out certain tasks in relation to these categories of persons. Of course, there were other situations as well; for example, providing security in terms of traffic. So these are some of the basic activities that the members of the Ministry of the Interior had in relation to these categories of persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the police also serve as guards to any of these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is precisely what I meant. Providing that kind of security for facilities, I meant, generally speaking, providing security, guards, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And would that be not only for prisoners of war camps but also for camps where civilians were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. There were situations like that as well and I said so in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to follow up on something that Judge Harhoff was asking you. At page 10, you made reference to the collection centres. And in your answer, you said: "The MUP did not have authority over such camps anywhere such as the Army of Republika Srpska did. There are instructions showing that it is the military organs that are in charge of such facilities carrying out tasks in a certain territory." Now, I want to talk about -- for now, I'm going to use the term collection centre and when I use that I'm thinking of a place where non-combatants are detained, so civilians, women, children, the elderly, non-fighters, people who have either, in some cases, I think, voluntarily shown up fleeing from areas of combat and others who have been removed and brought there by the military and/or the police because they were carrying out combat activities. Can you tell me what instructions you are talking about that gave the military the responsibility or put them in charge of such collection centres? Can you reference a document for us? I don't know what instructions you refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, while the witness is checking his documents, what is the page number you are referring to of Mr. Bajagic's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, of the transcript of his answer. Page 10, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, transcript, transcript. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed it is very difficult to give answers without being directed to a specific portion of the text from the report. However, I tried as fast as I could to come up with an effective answer to that question. It is an order based on International Humanitarian Law from the VRS in June 1992. Also, the 13th of June, 1992, is another reference and, generally speaking, there are many orders that came from the highest military organs and all of that is referred to in my footnote 333 through 345. There are many documents listed there and many legal regulations and bylaws that show in which way efforts were being made to organise the matters involved pertaining to these persons. If necessary, I can read out these footnotes, all of these documents that are contained in these footnotes and they have to do with paragraphs 291 onwards, practically until the end of this chapter. There are many orders of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska and the command of the Krajina Corps that speak of these matters on the basis of these general legal regulations that I mentioned first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at footnote 333 which is the order on the application of the International Law of War in the army, but I don't see anything in that. And I think it's Exhibit P1825, if Your Honours care to check. I don't see anything in that document that says the army is in charge of the collection centres. Would you like to see it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I liked anything, but if Mr. Bogdan Subotic, defence minister, issues an instruction on the 13th of June as to how detained persons should be treated, and that was in 1992 and that is in paragraph 293, then it is my understanding that the minister is issuing an instruction on the basis of which those are who -- those who are within his system have to behave, and that is the Army of Republika Srpska. It is clear enough to me, personally, that if the minister of defence issues such an instruction, then it's the Army of Republika Srpska that is in charge of such facilities. That is a logical conclusion, to my mind, and that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The instruction on the treatment of captured persons issued by the minister of defence on the 13th of June, 1992, is Exhibit P0189. Doesn't that document refer to prisoners of war because is the army capturing civilians? I take capture is in the course of combat and those persons would be prisoners of war; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. However, already on the 6 the of June, 1992, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska issued a directive strictly prohibiting, et cetera, et cetera, mistreatment of civilians, the unarmed population, and what is ordered is treating civilians on the basis of the Geneva Conventions. So if the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is issuing such a directive addressing military units on the ground, corps and everybody else, and if even the civilian population is mentioned in that directive, and the civilian population is not taking part in combat, on the basis of all of that I conclude that on certain situations on the ground the military was responsible for such categories of persons as well. That is how I can analyse documents. I don't know anything about the actual situation on the grounds, however on the basis of documents alone I can reach certain conclusions and that's the conclusion I reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll agree that sometimes it's risky to reach conclusions based on documents alone, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course you can interpret it that way as well, but I only did have documents, books, monographs, legal documents. On the basis of what else could I draw conclusions if it weren't for that material?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then let's look at this document and see if your conclusion was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P189, please. This is the 13 June 1992 document from Minister Subotic, the minister of defence, and it's talking about captured persons. If we could go to the last page. Okay. That's the reverse side of the document. Could we go back one page, I want to see the front page of this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a form that is attached with Minister Subotic's order about treatment of captured persons. And you see the card, it's a capture card for prisoner of war. It's not capture card for civilians. It's for a prisoner of war. Doesn't that suggest that this entire instruction from the minister relates to prisoners of war rather than civilians?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said. This document of the 13th of June has to do with prisoners of war. That is what I've been speaking about precisely, prisoners of war. And I relate it to this document. However, if you could have a look at the first page of this document, different terms are being used, not only POW camp but also collection centre, and that is why these terms appear in my report as well, the terms that appear in documents appear in my expert report too. This document has to do with prisoners of war since there is a card attached as well, however, the other document of the 6th of June has to do with civilian -- the civilian population as well on the basis of the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, in particular, I want to direct your attention to item number 2, which says: "Captured persons shall be taken to mean the members of enemy armed forces who have surrendered and laid down their arms or have been overpowered in or out of combat." Again that makes it clear this is about prisoners of war, not about civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, but I have to tell you that I'm not an expert in International Humanitarian Law of law of war within international law. However, I am educated enough to know that this has to do with prisoners of war, and I do know, basically, what prisoners of war are. I can give you no other comment with regard to this article except for saying that I take due note of what it says here and that I know that these are prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you look at paragraph 332 of your report. It's page 122 of the English and in the B/C/S it's page 104. And you mention in the middle of the paragraph about the gradual disbanding of prisoner of war camp, more specifically of Manjaca and Trnopolje. Was it my understanding, Professor, that Trnopolje was not a prisoner of war camp? Do you have information to the contrary that it was for prisoners of war rather than some sort of collection centre for civilians and non-combatants?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that when I read documents where these facilities are mentioned in relation to all the categories of persons who are in them, I did not deal in particular with the type and nature of the facilities involved. Not in such detail. However, you actually referred me to my paragraph 333, if I'm not mistaken, and you did not ask me to comment upon that. Am I supposed to? Or perhaps I didn't hear you right. What paragraph are you referring me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I meant to say 332 and that's what is in my English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I think you've answered my question. Now I want to talk about a different topic. Just in terms of style in your report, I note some places there will be text, and it's not a quote from a document, it appears to be just part of your conclusions or your statements of a premise that are underlined or in bold, which I understand to be you want to emphasise that. Is that standard practice in writing a report like this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's standard practice in writing reports like this here, but very often when I want to emphasise something, I use italics or I underline parts of the text or I use bold. That is done otherwise in various texts and books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. If you are quoting from a document and you typically as I see have it in quotation marks to indicate it's coming from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you have underlined or bolded something that's in quotation marks, can we take it that is in the original, otherwise you would note that it was emphasis added by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are situations when you quote something and that is sufficient to indicate the source. If there's a relevant footnote number and then if the document is referred to in the footnote, then you emphasise something additionally, but if you were to put parentheses each and every time after the text quoted, I think that technically that would burden the text as it were. I think that it's clear enough this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Don't you agree with me, as a general principle, if you've indicated something as a quotation that you shouldn't underline or bold with inside the quotation without making a note that emphasis has been added by you? Wouldn't you agree that's the better professional practice in writing a report or a monograph or a PhD thesis?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written many documents so far but there have been no such objections. It's a matter of convention and agreement. It's important to have a uniform practice. I don't see where the problem is when something is in inverted commas and italics. I don't see if -- that anything essential can change in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but the problem is, for example, at paragraph 159, which is page 66 of the English and I think it's page 56 of the B/C/S, you are quoting from, I think it's the constitution. Articles 80 and 81. And you have in quotation marks "activating the reserve police force in emergency situations." Is it underlined in the original or did you put that in because you wanted to emphasise the importance of this particular provision?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that here I speak about the MUP and in order to avoid inserting an additional paragraph, but with the intention to point out some facts, I underlined this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But wouldn't the better practice to have been then to put immediately after the underlined quotation in parentheses the words "emphasis added" so we would know that came from you and that was not in the original? Just makes it easier for the reader, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course your question presumes the universality of that practice which may not necessarily be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's why I'm trying to inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, but there are no universal criteria, that's what I can put to you. It's up to the author how he or she want to do it. If something is not in inverted commas when I put something in italics and I underlined it, then it was clear I was the one who did it, and this is all it means. Inverted commas mean this is a quotation, but you can also emphasise something by inverted commas, when you put something in italics without inverted commas or if you underline, it that means that the author signals the reader that a part of the text is more specific, but I don't see a problem with that. If there is a problem then I can apologise for underlining things. But the essence remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily suggesting a problem, I'm just trying to know what your practice is so when I read your report I know whether I need to go look at the original or if I can presume that something that's underlined in quotations is that way in the original. Now I know. Just have a look at footnote number 9. I have a question concerning how you cite sources, and it's page 7 in the English and I think it's page 6 in the B/C/S. One of the documents you referred to in this footnote is Goran Cular and Ivan Greguric, "How Cleavage Politics Survives Despite Everything: The case of Croatia," and you mention that's in a particular paper prepared for a workshop in Helsinki in 2007 taken from the Internet. I think this is document 65 ter 863D1. When I looked at that document, the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess could we have that up, that might be the best way to deal with it. 863D1 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if we have a B/C/S version or not, but for the Professor I know you read English. At the bottom of the cover page, it says, "First draft, please do not cite without author's permission." Did you get the author's permission for your use of this document in your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sources I find and that are on the Internet and that originate from some scientific or scholarly conferences are sources that I use. I don't think that's anything bad. I didn't take this text and translate it into Serbian, nor did I do anything else with it that goes contrary to some standards of conduct. If it can be found on a global information network, I see no reason why not to cite such a document. I see no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you don't know who -- you don't know how or who posted it on the Internet. That may have been someone who did so without getting the author's permission. But because it's on the Internet, you think it's okay, even though the document itself on the first page says, "Please do not cite without author's permission"? That's okay?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this is a first draft that you've shown, but on the Internet there is probably -- the proceedings can probably be found in which this -- of which this is also a part. I, again, don't think this is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Isn't the very fact that it's a first draft a possible reason that the author didn't want it cited without permission because it was still, in effect, a work in progress? That they didn't want it to be circulated without being checked with first?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, but I cite two sources for the remarks in my footnote. One of them is this one. I wanted to corroborate a statement with these two sources, a statement that was given long ago. On the Internet there are 5.000 different sources that refer to this sentence. I mentioned these two sources by the way in passing by, as it were, however, the contents of my paragraph on these sources are no secret at all. The proceedings in which this paper will be published certainly cannot change these facts. I can only repeat that I see no problem with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Professor. If we could look at paragraph 127 of your report. It's at page 44 and then 45 in B/C/S and English starts on page 51 but I want to talk about page 52. And here in paragraph 127, you are listing documents that are of "vital importance" for an overview and analysis of the establishment and development of the Serbian -- of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH, its remit, responsibilities, and organisation. And you list a number of documents. At the middle of page 52 in English and just above the middle in page 45 of the B/C/S, there are a series of, I think, 11 laws that you've listed which are from December 1993 and after. Did you think those were relevant to your report about the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the purposes of my report about the MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the laws and regulations that were created until the end of that calendar year are relevant, that is until the end of 1992. The same applies to the laws and regulations from the time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were in force, that had legal force and were applied to the work and functioning of the MUP of the Serb Republic, and the other documents are listed just to show the chronology that there was constant work on the improvement of the legal framework in another period as well. But it's only those documents that are important for this report and the analyses therein that were adopted -- or rather, that were created in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to talk a little bit about citations. There are a number of paragraphs in your report where there's no source footnoted. Now, I know in some of those paragraphs that's simply you stating your conclusions from an analysis of certain documents or perhaps setting out some background information to lay the framework for your next discussion, but would you agree it's generally best practice in a paper like this or report like this to have sources footnoted for all of your factual recitations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like you to direct me to a particular paragraph so I can comment on it. This kind of question, whether I would agree or not, well, it would be much better to be directed to a particular paragraph and then I'll try to give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's start out with paragraphs 81 through 84 where you are talking about the activities of the SDS. No footnotes for those four paragraphs. You feel it was not necessary?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. I thought I had one more I wanted to ask you about for the moment. Paragraph 257, which is at page 97 of the English and in the B/C/S page 82. And here you are talking about the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the last sentence in that paragraph says: "At the same time it is well known that the process of complete unification of the ARK and the SAO ...," which I take it to mean Serb autonomous regions or districts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "... into the state system of the Serbian Republic of BH was only completed at the beginning of 1993." No footnote for that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no footnote. That is what I state based on some 30 odd other paragraphs and some 30 or 40 documents with which I corroborated the statements in those paragraphs. It is very clear here in the entire paragraph 257, this is a conclusion of mine and I drew that conclusion from an analysis that I already made and I don't think that every paragraph must be footnoted. I tried to illustrate the chronology I speak about and all other problems with as many footnotes as possible, but in some paragraphs you simply don't feel the need to footnote it or otherwise you would repeat citing documents. But for what is stated in this paragraph, I felt it wasn't necessary to cite other sources. I have done so before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more on this topic. If we could look at paragraph 255, which is on page 96 of the English, and for you, Professor, it starts on page 81 and goes over to page 82 of the B/C/S. And here you are talking about re-subordination and you do have a footnote 279 for the first part of that paragraph, but if you could go to the last sentence, in my English translation it says: "Furthermore, a combat assignment may involve both direct combat and activities aimed at protecting communications and vital facilities and securing military facilities including camps and the like." But there's no citation for that. Is there a definition somewhere in the regulations or the laws that defines what a combat assignment is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in the laws and regulations that were in force at the time of the SFRY we could find a lot of that, but this sentence states what I have -- what I had already put forward based on a number of documents, and again, I don't see why I must footnote every sentence of my report. If I had known this to be a preference of yours then you would have dozens of footnotes to every sentence but I didn't want to burden my report in that manner. I would certainly have something to cite with regard to this, but this is merely a remark based on my analysis, and certainly a combat assignment can be any of these things mentioned. And the members of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH were re-subordinated to military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in that regard in this paragraph you have been talking about the Law on Internal Affairs which is Exhibit P530, the Law on Internal Affairs from 23 March 1992, as well as the order issued by Minister Stanisic on the 1st of May -- sorry, on the 15th of May, 1992, where he created war units within the MUP. And in those two documents it talks about the MUP being re-subordinated for combat operations or combat activities. Now, combat assignment is a term that's not exactly the same as a combat operation or a combat activity; is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the context in my own language, how you place it within a sentence. Sometimes combat activity or combat operation means direct participation in armed combat and sometimes it does not necessarily involve direct participation in armed combat. It depends on the context, it depends on how the commanders use it, how others use the term, and also what legal regulations say. So I always have to look at the context when a particular term is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, that's why I suggest it would be good to have a footnote here at the end of this paragraph to direct us to a regulation defining what kinds of things are combat activities, combat operations and combat assignments. But let me move on. Sorry, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had commented in this report what tasks were and what activities were, and so on and so forth, then the report should have been entitled differently. I focused on the Ministry of the Interior, not on military matters in this report. I only dealt with the military as much as it was necessary in order to shed more light on the position of the ministry in that period, not to deal with military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the first chapter of your report on the constituting the Serbian Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina and the establishment of organs of state authority, you have a lot of footnotes citing various media articles, books, Internet pages, and I wanted to ask you about a term that is used in a few places.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, what is the page of my report in B/C/S? Could you please give me a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just talking about, general, about chapter 1 which runs from page 3 to 39 in English. This is a section where you talk about the activities of the three nationalist parties, and I was making a point that you have a lot of references to media, Internet sources as well as books. And just at footnote 33, which is on page 16 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S, at the end of that footnote, you make reference to Domagoj Margetic, an article or book entitled, "Islamic Terrorism in the South of Europe: Zagreb S.N. 2006." S.N., is that a Latin term? Does that stand for "sin nombre," or something like that, meaning there's no publishers? Because I notice in your other citations at this general locations that would be the name of a publisher. What does S.N. stand for here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of this book published the book himself. It wasn't that some company published it for him. He is one of the most prominent Croatian journalists and researchers as concerns the periods of time that we are dealing with in this report too. He authored not only this book but also many others. However, this one is the most relevant one in this context, and that is why I include it in this report. It is most relevant for explaining the matters that we are dealing with. However, as I refer to that source, what I'm saying in this report is that other sources speak of the same facts from footnote 33 onwards. As I cross-reference these sources, they actually deal with the same subject matter. And I have no doubts as to the quality of this source. I personally do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This book by Mr. Margetic, Islamic terrorism, were you aware that it is dedicated to, among other persons, Dario Kordic, who was convicted in this Tribunal and sentenced to 25 years of imprisonment for war crimes? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't matter to me at all, what does matter is that Domagoj Margetic has a reputation as a journalist and as an author. Who the book is dedicated to, that, for me, is not of such importance. As I cross-reference the facts from Mr. Margetic's book with some others from Europe and America, I come to the conclusion that he is highly relevant for the things that he is writing about. Look at Sindler's book "Unfortunate Terror," look at "Terror in the Net of Evil," that is Ali Hamad and you will see that at least 90 per cent corresponds to the facts that are referred to in this paragraph. And many others, many foreign authors, foreign in relation to the country that I come from, speak of these things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, the Domagoj Margetic that we were just talking about before the break, that's the same Domagoj Margetic who was convicted of contempt of this Tribunal on the 7th of February, 2007, for publishing on his website the complete confidential list of witnesses in the Blaskic case and sentenced to three months in prison and a fine of 10.000 euros; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness's microphones are not on, I note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you turned them on now, Professor, your answer wasn't recorded. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of all those facts concerning Mr. Margetic. I did not really deal with his CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's not just a matter the of his CV, it was a matter of public record in this court. But you tell us you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that at all, that didn't really matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you telling me now knowing about it you still wouldn't perhaps have not used him as a footnoted source, just as a matter of judgement? You say there are plenty of sources for many of the things that you've cited him for, but given what arguably is reflected by the fact of his conviction and the underlying nature of that, don't you think that reflects something about his attitude, his bias, in regard to this Tribunal that might make him not the best source for you to use in your expert report in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether what you said about his offence is related to the content of the book that I cited. However, I would have quoted the book anyway. It's an open source. It was published publicly and many others have quoted it too. In that regard, I think that it is not a problem that I used this book as one of my sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is that your standard, if it's an open source and it's quoted by many others then it's good enough to go into your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if many people quote this book or, generally speaking, the number of quotations establishes its value in the scientific or professional market. If something is not quoted at all, then it is valueless in terms of content, the content of such a work. The index of quotation citation is one of the basic criteria in science, criteria for the quality of such a work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's talk about the use of media articles. In paragraph 25 of your report, that's page 11 of the English, page 10 in the B/C/S. Just past halfway down in that paragraph, you say: "Although newspaper comments are, generally and, in this case, specifically, an unfortunate choice of material for a detailed and objective analysis of the situation then in BH and the conduct of some political leaders, bearing in mind that Alija Izetbegovic in this statement illustratively indicated the direction of the work of his political party SDA and its activities on the formation of the Patriotic League paramilitary organisation, and it has been commented on in this report because it represents the only available material on Izetbegovic's statements on the topic from the period in question." I take that to mean that you think, generally, newspaper comments aren't a good source to use in a report like this; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all possibly used facts from newspaper articles such as statements, interviews, mono-views or other types of newspaper articles, I include all of that in that third category of material. My comment in this paragraph only has to do with the fact that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's -- that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic said something like this only once in the newspapers. I didn't find anything else about that but it's all in the context of the Patriotic League. However, you have this in this paragraph, these facts coming from direct participants in the establishment of the Patriotic League. You have sources speaking of its military obligation in this paragraph; however, it only has to do with the statement made by Alija Izetbegovic to the newspapers on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct in understanding that you think, generally speaking, that news articles are an unfortunate choice, but if it's the only source for a point you want to make, you are willing to use it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that, at least for purposes of illustration, this too can be used, but not only this for drawing final conclusions about some processes or events. I think that the previous paragraph, that is paragraph 24, with its sources that are footnoted are directly linked to Alija Izetbegovic's statement and they correspond with each other fully. It was in this sense that my statement should be understood that newspaper articles can be used as a tertiary source for the purpose of illustration to complete the picture of some events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And tertiary source, meaning the least reliable from primary to secondary to tertiary; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we cannot speak of the lowest level of reliability. If Mr. Izetbegovic, in June 1991, spoke about the activities from that period, that is June 1991, if he spoke about it in 1994 to the "Ljiljian" magazine, which was published in Sarajevo which was under the jurisdiction of the central authorities of Mr. Izetbegovic, I don't believe that he lied to this magazine. As a matter of fact, I think that he boasted about these facts rather than spoke or told lies. But I use this only as an illustration when I dealt with the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe one or two more sources. If you could look at footnote 33 in your report. It's page 16 of the English and page 12 going on to 13 of the B/C/S. I am sorry, I've got the -- page 16 of the English and it's on page 14 of the B/C/S. Here you are talking about -- in paragraph 36, you are talking about various Muslim organisations and connections to the SDA and secret arming of Muslims. Near the bottom, in what is footnoted as number 33, is an organisation that I can't pronounce. It's spelled M-u-w-a-f-a-q, Muwafaq foundation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your footnote you say that it was registered as a humanitarian organisation in Zagreb during 1992 as a branch office of the headquarters which operated out of London. The Tunisian Safiq Ayadi was at its helm, who was also known at INTERPOL for laundering Kuwaiti dinars which Iraq had seized during the attack on Kuwait. The main job of the organisation was to give logistic support to the TWRA humanitarian organisation and transfer terrorist from the RH to the BH. Now, what is the source in the footnote? What is the source for that information? Because the only thing that follows is compare Mr. Margetic's book and we've already talked about him. Does this text about this organisation and Mr. Ayadi come from that book or does it come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there's footnote, then it comes from that book. But, as I said, I could have cited another 50 sources for the same facts. As you see, you have read out the name of that alleged humanitarian organisation, but their connections with extremists are also mentioned, and that's the al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya. As far as I know, this is one of the 10 most dangerous terrorist organisations in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. You have a footnote then you have this text, following the text it says "compare," then you cite Mr. Margetic's book. To me, what I'm used to in reading a document, when there's footnote, then in the footnote there is a source for the item footnoted. But you have some text and you say "compare," that leads me to believe that what is written here is different somehow to something I might find in Mr. Margetic's book, it's confusing to me. How do you use the term "compare" in a footnote? Compare to what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The footnote first contains a text. I speak about the organisation briefly and then I refer the reader to the source to show that I haven't made up what I say but that it can be found in that source. This is exactly as it should be in a scholarly work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I would expect to see the text in the body of your document and then in the footnote just Mr. Margetic's work. Isn't that normally how you do it in the rest of your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's wrong. The footnotes sometimes only mention the source. Sometimes they can contain a comment about something without a source and other times it can contain both a comment and a text, the position of the author and then link that to another source and then it reads compare so and so, and that source then speaks about the same process, institution, or whatever. That's the structure of a footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's leave sources for now and talk about another issue with citations. Could you look at footnote 67, page 25 of the English, and in the B/C/S footnote 67 is at page 22. At the end of paragraph 51 you say: "How else but illegal and unconstitutional to call the fact that one Dzevad Tinjic from Zagreb, as far back as 10 April 1991, took over from the Crisis Staff of the Islamic community of the RH and Slovenia a considerable quantity of fire-arms and ammunition which was sent to BH for the secret arming of Muslims under the SDA's supervision." And then a footnote, you have a certification from Hasan Cengic to Mr. Tinjic for the purchase of weapons dated 3 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have up in e-court 65 ter number 739D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do we have a tab number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a Defence document, Your Honour. I don't recall what the tab number was on their list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's on the Stanisic Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's in the report. It's a footnote in his report and that's the 65 ter number of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe we announced this document to be used during our direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I announced I was going to use any document referred to in the expert's report. I don't have it on a separate list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question was only for easy referencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The original of this document is in German, but it appears it's from the 3rd of October, 1992, and I don't understand how this document supports that as far back as 10 April 1991 Mr. Tinjic took over fire-arms and ammunition. How does a statement from 7 December 1994 referring to some confirmation in October of 1992 take you back to April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat which footnote it is where I mention this source, the number of the footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Footnote 67.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the date that we can see at the top is the 3rd of October, 1992, but it isn't the dates that matter to me here but rather pointing out the fact, namely what Mr. Tinjic was doing. And this is just a confirmation of how those funds were transferred. His activities points at something. That mattered more to me than the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you seem to emphasise the date in your report and I note on the 3rd of October, 1992, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was at war actively with the VRS. What is inappropriate about Mr. Cengic paying for certain weapon in 1992 in October? And how did you link this to what you say is illegal activity in April 1991? There's no connection?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really inappropriate because a weapons embargo was in place imposed by the United Nations for all of former Yugoslavia. As far as I remember, I didn't deal with this matter personally here but it was the United Nations that imposed the embargo; that is, they banned any import of military equipment for the entire former SFRY. To me, this illustrates the fact that they acted in contravention of the decision of the United Nations organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not how you describe it in your report, and also, there's nothing in this document to indicate that these weapons were imported. You don't know whether or not they were manufactured within Bosnia, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was clear enough in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this fact -- and of course not every matter can be extensively dealt with in this report, so this is another opportunity to discuss that. It is obvious that this is not in Bosnia-Herzegovina but rather that some funds are transferred in different ways, and the United Nations imposed an embargo for the entire territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I can add one follow-up question to that. Mr. Bajagic, you write here, "As far back as 10 April 1991." Why did you emphasise this? Why did you say, "As far back as April 1991"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a precise answer now. If I stressed that, if I stressed the 10th of April, I could have cited another source which I probably had, but I can also make a mistake. But what mattered to me is what I already said. I may have omitted to cite another source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible too. That other source may have been more of a corroboration of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, I think I have maybe two more footnotes I want to ask you about and the next one is footnote 64, which we find on page 24 of the English, page 21 of the B/C/S. This is the last footnote to your paragraph 47 which begins a couple of pages earlier. And paragraph 47 is about the activities of the Mujahedin, and you say: "We will mention the names of some of the most well known terrorists who were active members of the El Mujahid unit." Then you've got a list of, I think, by my count 27 named individuals whose names are in bold, I note, I guess because you want to bring special attention to them. Footnote 64 says: "This is just a shortlist of the names of terrorists who took an active part in the war in BH on the side of the BH Army and under the direct patronage of Alija Izetbegovic and his political party, the SDA, and who were woven into the fabric of terrorist groups under Bin Laden's leadership out of which today's well known al-Qaeda was created." Then you say four more, see Galijasevic's book. Now again that's four more. But for this part, where you say this is just a shortlist, are those your words or does that come from some other source or does that come from Galijasevic's book?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text in the footnote up until the mention of the source is my comment. And this is but a shortlist of names and I refer the reader to the source where he or she can read hundreds or more of these names on over 20 pages, the names of these same persons and others who were members of the El Mujahedin or El Mujahid detachment. Mr. Galijasevic mentions that in his book on pages 114 through 137, and we can find the complete list of names of the members of various terrorist organisations who were active in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and were members of the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I note that this is in your chapter 1 of your report which is about the constituting of the Serbian Republic. You think it was necessary to include the names of those who apparently their only activity was in 1994 or 1995? Because this seems to be a section talking about 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activities of many who are listed here started in 1992, not from 1994 or 1995. I could have quoted the source Ali Hamad "In the Net of Evil" and you could have seen that that and many other sources show that these persons and their comrades in arms operated already in 1992 in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I had in mind was a general political context, and that for that purpose it was necessary to devote a few paragraphs to this question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A few paragraphs, I note that this section listing the 47 names is as long as your entire section on the SDS and its activities. Don't you think that reflects a bias on your part that this single paragraph is as long as your entire section about the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph is long but only from a technical point of view because there is a list of names and the terrorist organisations that these people come from. It may be considered over-extensive but the names from this list are not unimportant. I have already said that in addition to -- apart from this paragraph throughout this report I deal with the activities of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. It's not only one particular part of the first chapter. So except for this, the entire report is dedicated to the activities of the Serb side and in that relation I see no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Of the 27 names cited in paragraph 47, I see there are footnotes for 10 of them, I guess, to support the information that is supplied after their names, but for 17 of them there are no footnotes and I know you just said a little bit ago suggesting that most of these guys were active in 1992. I'd like you to look at a few names in particular and tell me if you can give us any additional information. At the bottom of page 20 in your B/C/S, and this is on page 23 about four names up from the bottom in English, the name Abdulah Essindar, it says, from the state of Yemen, a warrant for his arrest has been issued for a car bomb in Rijeka in 1995. He is a member of the Mujahedin community in Bocinja. What does that have to do with -- about any alleged activity by him in the war in Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every one of these names mentioned here took active part in the war in Bosnia. This is just additional information. Just as I put an abbreviation after a particular name, in parenthesis indicating that person's membership in a terrorist organisation. So this is just additional information. This goes in general terms for all the persons I refer to here from the first paragraph onwards. They were all members of the El Mujahedin unit and this is some more specific information about each and every one of them that I came across as I was looking into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us any information about when and where he was supposedly active in the Mujahedin unit? You don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sources I used directed me to that, namely to put his name on the list of active participants. I know that on the basis of the sources I read and that indicate his name as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But does it indicate when and where precisely he was active?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for all the activities of that unit and other units, it's not only one, there is an entire book that describes that. Ali Hamad, "In the Net of Evil," that's the book, and John Sindler in his book on terror speaks about this as well, as do a few other books that I use as a source and that are listed in the footnotes to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next two names on the list, Imad Ai Husin, Karray Kamel Ben Ali, also known as Abu Hamza. There's nothing here in your report about when and where they would have been active in Bosnia, is there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The beginning of paragraph 47, I say that I'm mentioning some of the most important terrorists who are members of the El Mujahedin unit and then I provide their names, and it is all based on the sources referred to in the following footnotes. For a particular person, I could not research his entire CV but everyone says that this specific person was a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Everyone says, that's little far reaching, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, okay, far reaching. He is mentioned in sources, as stated in the footnotes. Even one source is sufficient for me to be able to use that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I realise you've told us that before. Paragraph 80 of your report, which page 32 of the B/C/S and starts on page 36 and goes on to 37 of the English. I want to quote part of that for you. You mention: "The unjustifiably accepted views that only the Serbian side in BH in the 1991/1992 period aspired to the break-up of BH and that the chief force in these endeavours were Serbian personnel in the SRBH MUP. And later also the newly formed MUP of the Serbian Republic." I want to be clear I understand, is your complaint a bit -- I guess it goes basically to two things. You are complaining that some people have the unjustified view that only the Serbian side aspire to break up BH; is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not complaining. I'm presenting a statement, a final statement on the basis of the preceding analysis of the past 10 or 15 paragraphs, that is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's your opinion, right, that those who accept the view that only the Serbian side aspire to break up is unjustified; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you and I will probably agree about this, that there were others who also aspired to the break up of BH, SDA, certain members of the SDA, certain members of the HDZ; agreed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said in my report that I believe that all three sides were active in that direction and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you willing to agree with me that certain members, certain Serb personnel in the MUP were a force in those endeavours, not necessarily the chief force but a force in such endeavours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the official documentation of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of BH and the positions that I analysed, or rather, the remarks made by the top personnel of the MUP at different collegium meetings, I did not see that that could be said, that they were the main force or chief force. Perhaps some individuals on the ground may be referred to in that context, but in the official documentation that I used, or rather the sources, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But we talked about before the draft MUP annual report for April through December of 1992 which Dr. Nielsen referred to extensively in his report, and you are aware that in sections of that report, MUP's own report, it talks about the illegal activities of some of their members in preparing for the break-up of the original joint MUP; right? You are aware of that? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were such comments, but in my entire report I do not speak about the break up of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of BH. I speak about a completely different process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move now to your annexes. You told us before about how these came to be attached to your report, and the first one I want to talk about is Annex 12, which you told us was the late edition based on a request by the Defence team, talking about subordination of the police to the army. Now, I note that annex has 19 paragraphs in total, and I see that there are only six footnotes which relate to paragraphs 3, 5, and 6. Can I take it then that the rest of the content in those other 16 paragraphs is basically your bare, unsupported opinion about how things worked because you don't cite any documents for those other paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere do I refer to bare opinions, this report included. Everything I state is based on my scientific experience. I repeat once again, I wrote Annex 12 as an integral text, a very brief text, because this could be expanded on further. These are points rather than classical paragraphs that will probably provide a better overview of what I was trying to say. If there is no numeric reference, all that does not mean that this is just a question of me presenting my arbitrary assessments. These are, rather, comments on Official Gazettes, laws on defence, and something that I, of course, as a man who is involved in science, can present here as his general sublimated knowledge without mentioning many and many sources, a multitude of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to confirm that you didn't read the Prosecution's expert Mr. Ewan Brown's report about the army, did you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if I asked you this before, but did you read the VRS, Bosnian Serb army's own report on combat readiness, summarising their activities from their creation in May 1992 through the rest of the year 1992? Did you read that document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've already said that I haven't read Mr. Brown's report or any other expert report and I haven't read this document of the Army of Republika Srpska either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And other than your mandatory military service you did, I think, in 1980 and 1981 for about a year, you have no other military service; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your time that you were an active member of the MUP from April 1992 through the end of 1995, were you personally ever re-subordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think I have a couple of other annexes I want to ask you about. Annex number 3 is a -- is at 159 of the English, I'm not sure which page in the B/C/S. It's a decision on the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna of 18 November 1991, and your footnote for this document makes reference to the Official Gazette, I think it's Exhibit 1D141.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have 1D141 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, let me refresh my memory. I think you told us that these annexes, you did not attach a copy of the original document but instead you typed it up yourself, is that how these were prepared?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I typed the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire, is this the only pages of this exhibit or if we could go to the next page. It makes reference to an enclosure. I don't know if that is attached or not. Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, here on the screen we see the document and we have on this page nine articles, I think it actually goes on one more page to ten articles. Your Annex number 3 only has eight articles. Can you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this happened. It's a technical mistake. But you have the original document here so that doesn't change anything essential with regard to this annex. What was shown to me was not the Official Gazette of the HZ HB from September 1992 but a different document from e-court, but if my -- but if in my text Articles 9 and 10 are missing, that doesn't change anything essential because we have the original here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the point is you told us you created these annexes and you selected the documents for the annexes because you thought they were the most important and that you wanted the Judges to be able to see those documents in their entirety. So how can you now say it's not important that you don't have the full document in your annex because that's the one you wanted to draw the Judges' attention to? That's negligent at best, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. It is negligent. And I do not know how this could happen. Article 9 reads that this decision enters into force immediately and then there's Article 10 that follows, but the mistake is obviously due -- is of a technical nature and not the result of some intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to object until this moment because I wanted the witness to finish his response. However, I note that 482 is the decision printed in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna. What Mr. Hannis is showing to the witness is a document I had shown to the witness which is FN footnote 71/1 of this -- of his report. Now, if Mr. Hannis wants to cross-examine the witness, he must show in the proper document referred to in the footnote. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then, can we have is look at -- it was my understanding that the document in footnote 71 is 1D41. Is that not correct? I'd be happy to look at the Official Gazette if we have it available. Can my learned friend help me, is it something else other than 1D41?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
